orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, continuing her story to Lockwood. Several years pass at Wuthering Heights while old Mr. Earnshaw's health fails. Scholars date his death, at the end of this chapter, to October 1777.

notes.g: Stuck in his seat by the fire.
notes.n: Old farmhouse fireplaces often had a seat built into the corner beside them, the warmest spot for an old or sick person.

notes.g: Anything he thought was disrespect to his position as master.
Take advantage of, or boss around.

notes.m: To 'humour' someone is to indulge their wishes. 'Partiality' means favouring one person.

notes.n: Curates were often poorly paid, so this one also taught children and farmed.

notes.g: Made his church income enough to live on.
notes.m: 'Answer' here means 'be sufficient'. The 'living' is his church post and its pay (see Chapter III).

notes.g: The Linton children of Thrushcross Grange.
notes.n: The first mention of the Lintons in Nelly's story. Remember 'Catherine Linton' on the window ledge.

notes.g: Sent away to study at a university.

notes.tr: Hindley is good for nothing, and will never do well, wherever he goes.

notes.n: In the Gospels, the Pharisees are shown as strict about religious rules but proud and uncharitable. Jesus criticises them often.

notes.t: ransacked a Bible to rake the promises to himself and fling the curses to his neighbours
notes.g: Searched the Bible for blessings to claim for himself and curses to throw at everyone else.
notes.n: A sharp picture of Joseph's harsh religion: God's favour is for him, punishment is for others.

notes.g: The state of his soul, and whether it would be saved.

notes.n: The same Calvinist word young Mrs. Heathcliff threw back at Joseph in Chapter II.
Like the highest point the tide reaches.

notes.t: A wild, wicked slip she was
notes.g: She was a wild, naughty little thing.
notes.m: A 'slip' of a girl is a slim young girl. Nothing to do with slipping.

notes.g: Play at being the bossy lady of the house.
In the best years of his life.
Teasing me to provoke a reaction.
notes.n: From 'bear-baiting', a cruel sport of setting dogs on a chained bear.

notes.g: Mock rudeness (which her father thought was real).
Commands; what she told him to do.

notes.t: I cannot love thee, thou’rt worse than thy brother
notes.g: I can't love you, you're worse than your brother.
notes.n: 'Thee', 'thou' and 'thy' are the old familiar forms of 'you' and 'your'. Yorkshire country people still used them, especially to children and family.

notes.m: In northern speech 'I doubt' means 'I'm afraid that', not 'I don't believe'.

notes.t: the servants generally sat in the house then
notes.g: In those days the servants sat with the family in the main living room ('the house').
notes.n: An older, more countrified way of living. Grander homes kept servants separate.

notes.m: In Yorkshire speech 'rarely' could mean 'very much, splendidly', not 'seldom'.

notes.g: Can you not; why can't you.
Finished reading his chapter of the Bible.

notes.tr: Get yourselves upstairs and keep quiet. You can say your prayers on your own this evening. I've got something to do.
notes.n: Nelly reports Joseph's words, keeping his dialect.

notes.g: The nearest village, with the church, doctor and parson.
notes.n: Like 'Gimmerden Sough' in Chapter III, an invented place name.
Joseph wants him to pray over the body. Nelly can't see what use a doctor or a parson could be now.

notes.t: comforting each other with better thoughts
notes.g: The two children comfort each other by imagining heaven.
notes.n: Remember this scene of Catherine and Heathcliff alone together. Catherine's diary in Chapter III was written soon after this death ('T' maister nobbut just buried').
